recipes.title: Kansas City Brisket Burnt Ends
recipes.blurb: Cubes of the fatty brisket point, sauced and put back in the smoke until they tighten into sticky, candied bites. Barbecue people call them meat candy and they are not exaggerating.

items: 1 brisket point, also called the deckle (5 lb / 2.3 kg)
2 tbsp (30 ml) yellow mustard, as a binder
3 tbsp (20 g) coarsely ground black pepper
4 or 5 chunks oak, hickory, or pecan wood (about 1 lb / 450 g)
1 cup (240 ml) water, in a spray bottle for spritzing
1 cup (240 ml) thick tomato-based barbecue sauce
⅓ cup (75 g) light brown sugar, packed
4 tbsp (55 g) unsalted butter, cut into pats
1 tbsp of the same rub, reserved from above

instructions.title: Get the right cut
instructions.text: Ask the butcher for the brisket point or deckle, which is the thick, fatty muscle that sits on top of the flat on a whole packer. If they only sell whole packers, buy one and separate the two muscles along the fat seam yourself. The point is far fattier than the flat, and that fat is exactly what renders into the sticky texture burnt ends need.

instructions.title: Trim, but not too much
instructions.text: Trim the outer fat cap down to about ¼ inch (6 mm) and cut away any hard, waxy fat, but leave the interior marbling alone. Square off thin edges so nothing hangs out to burn. Over-trimming is the classic mistake here: without internal fat you get dry brown cubes instead of glossy ones.

instructions.title: Season the night before
instructions.text: Mix the black pepper, salt, and garlic powder and set 1 tbsp aside for the sauce later. Coat the point with the mustard and press the rest of the rub on heavily from every angle, including the underside. Refrigerate uncovered on a rack for 8 to 24 hours; the salt penetrates and the surface dries so the bark can set.

instructions.title: Set the smoker
instructions.text: Bring your smoker to a steady 250°F (120°C) at grate level and add two wood chunks once the coals are ashed over. Wait for thin blue smoke before the meat goes on, since thick white smoke will make everything taste acrid. Fill a water pan if your cooker has one, which helps hold humidity and steadies the temperature.

instructions.title: Smoke it whole
instructions.text: Put the point on fat side up and smoke it whole for about 5 hours, spritzing lightly with water after the third hour. Do not cube it yet — cutting early exposes too much surface and dries the meat out. Add one more wood chunk at the 2-hour mark if the smoke has thinned out.

instructions.title: Push through the stall
instructions.text: The internal temperature will stall somewhere between 150 and 165°F (65 and 74°C), often for two hours. This is evaporative cooling and it is completely normal, so hold your fire steady rather than raising it. If you are pressed for time, wrap the point in butcher paper once the bark is dark and firm and it will push through in about half the time.

instructions.title: Cook to 195°F
instructions.text: Continue until the point reaches 195 to 200°F (91 to 93°C) and a probe slides into the thickest part with only slight resistance. You want it just short of fully tender, since it has another 90 minutes of cooking ahead of it in the sauce. Total time is usually 5 to 6 hours at 250°F (120°C).

instructions.title: Rest, then cube
instructions.text: Let the point rest 20 minutes on a board so it firms up enough to cut cleanly. Slice it into even 1½-inch (4 cm) cubes, which is big enough that they do not dry out and small enough that every cube gets sauce on all six sides. Even sizing matters more than exact size, because mixed sizes cook unevenly.

instructions.title: Sauce and pan them
instructions.text: Toss the cubes in a disposable foil pan with the barbecue sauce, brown sugar, honey, cider vinegar, and the reserved 1 tbsp of rub until every piece is coated. Dot the pats of butter over the top. Spread them into a single layer so they roast rather than stew in a pile.

instructions.title: Finish uncovered
instructions.text: Put the pan back in the 250°F (120°C) smoker, uncovered, for 60 to 90 minutes, stirring gently every 30 minutes. The sauce will reduce and cling, the edges will darken, and the cubes will go from wet to tacky. They are done when a cube lifted on a fork holds a glossy coat that does not run off.

instructions.title: Taste and serve hot
instructions.text: Pull one cube out and cut it in half: the inside should be juicy and the fat fully rendered with no chewy white streaks left. If it is still firm, give it another 20 minutes covered with foil. Serve them straight from the pan while they are hot, with toothpicks and plenty of napkins.

tips: Make-ahead: smoke the point a day early, refrigerate it whole, then cube, sauce, and finish the next day. Cold meat cubes even more neatly.
Poor man's burnt ends use a 4 lb (1.8 kg) chuck roast the exact same way and cost half as much. They are excellent, just a little less fatty.
If the cubes come out dry, you trimmed too much fat or overcooked the point before cubing. Pull it at 195°F (91°C), not 205°F (96°C).
Do not cover the pan during the finishing stage. Covering traps steam and gives you saucy stew meat instead of candied edges.
recipes.keyTemp: Smoke the point to 195 to 200°F (91 to 93°C) before cubing, then finish in sauce until the fat is fully rendered.
recipes.pairing: Creamy potato salad, baked beans, white bread, and a cold bourbon and Coke.

recipes.title: Char Siu Chinese Barbecue Pork
recipes.blurb: Strips of pork shoulder marinated overnight in hoisin, five-spice, and honey, then roasted until the edges char and the glaze turns to red lacquer. It is the sweet-savory pork that hangs in every Chinatown window.

items: 2 lb (900 g) boneless pork shoulder, cut into strips 2 in (5 cm) wide and 1½ in (4 cm) thick
1 cup (240 ml) water, for the roasting pan, plus up to ½ cup (120 ml) more to top it up
2 tbsp (30 ml) Shaoxing wine or dry sherry
½ tsp (1 g) ground white pepper
2 cubes red fermented bean curd plus 1 tsp of its brine, optional
2 tbsp reserved marinade, boiled for 2 full minutes

instructions.title: Cut the pork into strips
instructions.text: Trim the shoulder of any thick fat sheets but leave the marbling, then cut it with the grain into long strips about 2 inches (5 cm) wide and 1½ inches (4 cm) thick. Strips give you far more surface area than a roast, which is where the charred, caramelized edges come from. Uniform thickness matters more than uniform length so everything finishes together.

instructions.title: Mix the marinade
instructions.text: Whisk the hoisin, soy sauce, Shaoxing wine, oyster sauce, sugar, honey, garlic, five-spice, and white pepper in a bowl until smooth. If you are using red fermented bean curd, mash the cubes with the brine first until they dissolve — this is what gives authentic char siu its reddish color and savory funk, not food coloring. Taste it: it should be aggressively sweet and salty, since it has to season the whole strip.

instructions.title: Reserve and marinate
instructions.text: Set aside ¼ cup (60 ml) of the marinade in a covered container in the fridge for the glaze later. Put the pork strips in a zip-top bag with the rest, press out the air, and massage it until every surface is coated. Refrigerate at least 12 hours and up to 24, turning the bag once or twice.

instructions.title: Bring the pork to room temperature
instructions.text: Take the bag out 45 minutes before roasting so the strips are not fridge-cold going into a hot oven. Cold meat browns unevenly and takes longer, which risks drying out the thinner ends. Meanwhile, take the reserved marinade out too.

instructions.title: Set up the pan
instructions.text: Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C) with a rack in the upper third. Line a rimmed sheet pan with foil, pour in the 1 cup (240 ml) of water, and set a wire rack over it. The water catches the sugary drips and keeps them from burning into acrid smoke, which is the single most common char siu problem at home.

instructions.title: Roast the first side
instructions.text: Shake the excess marinade off each strip and lay them on the rack with at least 1 inch (2.5 cm) between them. Roast for 15 minutes, until the surface is dry to the touch and starting to darken at the corners. Space matters — strips that touch will steam instead of roasting.

instructions.title: Boil the reserved marinade
instructions.text: While the pork roasts, pour the reserved ¼ cup (60 ml) of marinade into a small saucepan and boil it hard for a full 2 minutes. It touched raw pork, so it must be boiled before it goes anywhere near cooked meat. Take 2 tbsp of it, whisk in the 3 tbsp honey and 1 tbsp hot water, and you have your glaze.

instructions.title: Flip and roast again
instructions.text: Turn each strip over with tongs and roast 15 minutes more. The pork should be firming up and the edges going deep brown-red. If the water in the pan has evaporated, add another ½ cup (120 ml) so the drippings never scorch.

instructions.title: Glaze in layers
instructions.text: Brush the strips with a thin coat of glaze and roast 5 minutes, then flip, glaze the other side, and roast 5 minutes more. Repeat once more if you want a heavier lacquer, watching closely because honey burns quickly at 425°F (220°C). Thin repeated coats build a glossy shell; one thick coat just slides off.

instructions.title: Check the temperature
instructions.text: Push a thermometer into the thickest strip. Char siu is taken further than a pork chop on purpose, to 160°F (71°C), because shoulder has enough fat and collagen that the extra heat makes it tender rather than dry. Whole-muscle pork is safe at 145°F (63°C) with a 3-minute rest, so anything from there up is fine — 160°F (71°C) is simply where the texture is best.

instructions.title: Char the edges
instructions.text: Move the pan 6 inches (15 cm) under the broiler for 1 to 2 minutes per side, watching it every second. You are after blackened tips and blistered edges, which is where the name char siu comes from. There is a 20-second window between beautifully charred and burnt, so do not answer your phone.

instructions.title: Rest and slice
instructions.text: Rest the strips on a board for 10 minutes so the juices settle and the glaze sets into a tacky shell. Slice across the grain about ¼ inch (6 mm) thick; each slice should have a dark ring and a rosy interior. Brush the slices with any leftover glaze and serve warm over rice or in steamed buns.

tips: Pork shoulder is the right cut — it has the fat to stay juicy through a hot roast. Tenderloin makes a dry, disappointing char siu no matter how carefully you cook it.
Maltose is the traditional glaze sugar and gives an unmistakable sheen. It is rock-hard in the jar, so warm the jar in hot water for 5 minutes before you try to scoop it.
Make-ahead: char siu keeps 4 days refrigerated and freezes for 2 months. Slice cold, then warm it in a hot pan for 60 seconds a side.
Leftovers are the whole point for a lot of people. Dice them into fried rice, tuck them into steamed bao, or lay slices over a bowl of wonton noodle soup.
Red fermented bean curd is worth seeking out at an Asian grocery, but the recipe is still excellent without it — just expect a browner, less crimson color.
recipes.keyTemp: Roast to 160°F (71°C) for the best texture on pork shoulder; the food-safety minimum for whole-muscle pork is 145°F (63°C) plus a 3-minute rest.
recipes.pairing: Steamed jasmine rice, blanched gai lan with oyster sauce, and jasmine tea or a cold pilsner.

recipes.title: Italian Sausage and Peppers
recipes.blurb: One skillet, forty easy minutes, and the smell that takes over a street fair. Brown the sausages, soften the peppers in their fat, and let a splash of wine pull it all together.

items: 6 links Italian sausage, sweet or hot (1½ lb / 680 g total)
2 bell peppers, one red and one yellow, sliced ½ in (1 cm) thick (about 4 cups / 400 g)
1 large yellow onion, sliced ½ in (1 cm) thick (about 2 cups / 250 g)
½ tsp (1 g) red pepper flakes
¾ tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
½ tsp (1 g) coarsely ground black pepper
½ cup (120 ml) dry white wine or low-sodium chicken stock
2 tbsp chopped fresh basil or flat-leaf parsley
4 hoagie or Italian rolls, split and warmed

instructions.title: Do not prick the sausages
instructions.text: Leave the links whole and resist the urge to poke holes in them, which is a myth that only lets fat and juice escape. Pat them dry with a paper towel so they brown rather than steam. If the links are very thick, more than 1¼ inches (3 cm), leave them whole anyway and just plan on a couple of extra minutes.

instructions.title: Brown the sausages
instructions.text: Heat 1 tbsp of the olive oil in a 12-inch (30 cm) skillet over medium heat until it shimmers, then add the links in a single layer. Cook 8 to 10 minutes total, turning every 2 minutes, until they are browned on all sides but still slightly underdone in the middle. Medium heat, not high, is the key here — high heat splits the casings and pushes all the fat out at once.

instructions.title: Set them aside
instructions.text: Move the browned sausages to a plate; they will finish cooking in the peppers later. Leave every drop of rendered fat in the pan, because that seasoned fat is what the vegetables cook in and it carries all the fennel and garlic flavor from the sausage. Add the second tablespoon of oil only if the pan looks dry.

instructions.title: Cook the onions first
instructions.text: Add the sliced onion with the ¾ tsp salt and cook over medium-high heat for 4 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the edges start to brown and the slices soften. Salting now pulls water out and speeds up the browning. Scrape the bottom as you go to lift the browned sausage bits.

instructions.title: Add the peppers
instructions.text: Add the sliced bell peppers and cook 5 to 6 minutes more, stirring every minute or so. You want them softened and blistered in spots but still holding their shape, not collapsed into mush. If the pan looks crowded, that is fine — they will shrink by nearly half as they cook.

instructions.title: Bloom the aromatics
instructions.text: Push the vegetables to the edges of the pan, add the sliced garlic, oregano, red pepper flakes, and black pepper to the center, and stir them in the hot fat for 45 seconds until fragrant. Garlic burns in about 90 seconds at this heat, so keep it moving and do not let it go past pale gold. Then stir everything together.

instructions.title: Cook the tomato paste
instructions.text: Clear another small space, add the tomato paste, and let it fry for 90 seconds, stirring, until it darkens from bright red to brick. This drives off the raw canned flavor and deepens the whole dish. Stir it through the vegetables so they take on a rusty coating.

instructions.title: Deglaze and finish the sausages
instructions.text: Pour in the wine and scrape the bottom of the pan clean with a wooden spoon while it bubbles. Nestle the sausages back in with any juices from the plate, turn the heat to medium-low, cover, and simmer 6 to 8 minutes. The steam finishes cooking the sausages through while the peppers turn silky.

instructions.title: Check and serve
instructions.text: Cut into the thickest sausage or probe it: fresh pork sausage needs 160°F (71°C) in the center and should show no pink. Taste the peppers and add salt in pinches until they taste bright rather than flat, then scatter the basil over the top. Pile everything into warm split rolls, or serve it over polenta with the pan juices spooned on.

tips: Mix sweet and hot links — three of each — so everyone at the table gets what they want without you making two pans.
Make-ahead: the whole dish reheats well and is arguably better the next day. Keep the rolls separate and warm them fresh.
For a saucier version, add a 14 oz (400 g) can of crushed tomatoes with the wine and simmer 15 minutes instead of 8.
Leftovers make a great baked ziti: slice the sausages into coins, toss with the peppers and a pound of cooked pasta, top with mozzarella, and bake at 375°F (190°C) for 20 minutes.
recipes.keyTemp: Fresh pork sausage is done at 160°F (71°C) in the center, with no pink remaining.
recipes.pairing: Crusty rolls or soft polenta, a simple green salad, and a glass of Chianti or a cold Peroni.
